conventions.convention: The state set may be empty; every statewise action set is finite and nonempty. Rewards have a finite real alphabet and a joint next-state/reward law. Reward and next state need not be independent.
For an empty state set, the value-function space is a singleton, its sup metric and sup norm are zero, and Bellman operators are its unique self-map.
Discounts satisfy 0 ≤ γ < 1. Reward sequences start at index 1, discount powers start at index 0, the N-term partial sum is empty at N=0, and γ⁰=1 even for γ=0.

Nonempty-state policy path laws assume the Axiom of Choice. The reward-state chain starts at (s,0), where 0 is a dummy reward; the first return reward is R₁. Empty-state values require no path law or Choice.
Policy iteration evaluates policies exactly, retains every currently greedy action, and otherwise selects the earliest maximizing action in a supplied finite action list.
Value iteration takes an integer iteration budget m≥0 and returns V_m; its procedure does not claim convergence in finitely many iterations.
The policy-improvement theorem compares expected discounted values of stationary policies; deterministic policies are embedded as point-mass stationary policies.

load_bearing.statement: A finite MDP has a finite state set S, possibly empty, finite nonempty action sets A(s), a finite real reward alphabet, and nonnegative joint masses p(s′,ρ|s,a) summing to one for each admissible pair. Expected rewards and state-transition probabilities are the corresponding finite sums.

For a finite MDP and 0≤γ<1, every stationary-policy Bellman operator and the Bellman optimality operator satisfy the sup-norm contraction inequality with constant γ. Each has exactly one fixed point in the real-valued functions on S.

For M≥0, 0≤γ<1, and any real sequence with |ρ_j|≤M, the series ∑_{j≥0}γʲρ_{j+1} converges absolutely. Its sum and every partial sum have absolute value at most M/(1−γ), and the remainder after N terms is at most Mγᴺ/(1−γ), including N=0.
For any finite set S, the real-valued functions on S form a complete metric space under the maximum absolute coordinate difference, with distance zero on the singleton function space when S is empty.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For a finite MDP with nonempty S and a stationary Markov policy, the policy mixture of the joint reward-transition law defines a probability kernel on S×(R∪{0}); from every (s,0) there is a path law whose coordinate process is a homogeneous chain with that kernel relative to its natural filtration.

For a finite MDP, 0≤γ<1, and any stationary Markov policy π, the expected discounted state value satisfies T^π V^π=V^π. The empty-state case needs no Choice; otherwise Choice is assumed for the path-law definition.

Under the stated discounted finite-MDP hypotheses and Choice in the nonempty-state branch, a deterministic policy greedy with respect to V^π weakly improves every state value. A strict one-step improvement gives a strict value improvement. Exact tie-retaining policy iteration makes at most N_det−1 changes and terminates at a deterministic policy with value V*, which dominates every stationary-policy value.

concerns.concern: Proof 1.1 establishes convergence of the absolute-value series and concludes absolute convergence. Proof 2.1 then says the signed finite tail sums converge to G 'by step 1.1', without supplying the implication from absolute convergence to convergence. That implication is not part of the cited def-series or comparison theorem. The existing published lem-absolute-convergence-implies-convergence, opened for this check, supplies exactly the missing implication but is absent from deps and Facts. The claim is true; this is a short missing justification before G and its tail limits are used.

Fact F4 attributes 'the absolute value of a finite sum is at most the sum of the absolute values' to lem-of-abs-value and lem-finite-sum-laws. Neither cited statement supplies the triangle inequality: lem-of-abs-value states positivity, separation, sign bounds, symmetry and multiplicativity, while lem-finite-sum-laws states algebra and order rules. The opened published lem-triangle-inequality-finite supplies the exact inequality but is absent from this item's deps and F4. Steps 1.2 and 2.1 use that inequality.

seams_checked.note: Checked the actual finite-MDP, path-law, policy-value, Bellman-fixed-point and bounded-return citations in the tabular definitions, algorithms and relevant proofs. They preserve the joint finite reward-transition law and discount range. Path-law/value consumers state Choice; the greedy-policy lemma proves the stronger adapted-continuation optimality claim locally.

The bounded-reward definition explicitly identifies its Borel [0,1] reward law as an extension of the supplier's finite reward alphabet. It imports the finite state/action and joint-law conventions, rather than treating the discounted-return results as average-reward theorems. The communicating/diameter definition preserves legal statewise actions.

The learned-model definition faithfully derives expected rewards and state marginals from the joint law. The stochastic-shortest-path definition supplies its own absorbing-goal and positive-cost assumptions. Dyna-Q explicitly restricts its stored-response model to deterministic dynamics and rewards; it does not import an unsupported discounted convergence claim.

The finite-POMDP definition faithfully imports the joint next-state/reward masses and their marginals, with a common finite action set as a special case. Its finite-horizon allowance γ=1 is stated locally and does not invoke the supplier's infinite discounted-return theorem.

The finite-horizon occupancy lemma and imitation-learning definition use the actual normalized transition marginals and stationary-policy rows. Their finite-sum occupancy construction explicitly avoids an infinite-path extension, so it does not silently inherit a path-law conclusion without Choice.

The CMDP definition preserves the nonempty finite state/action/reward model and joint masses. The occupancy proof establishes normalization of finite-time masses before applying the bounded-return lemma to bounded deterministic sequences of expected transition signals. The discounted-cost definition distinguishes expected constraints from trajectory bounds.
